title: How To Strengthen Your Students’ Focus And Improve Behavior
author: Michael Linsin
summary: In an era of smartphones and constant digital distraction, Linsin argues that the ability to focus on one task for an extended period is becoming a rare and valuable skill, and that lengthy independent practice is a core SCM principle for building it. He recommends building this stamina gradually—starting with a modest amount of independent work time, such as ten minutes, and adding a minute per week until diminishing returns appear, at which point teachers should hold steady for a few weeks. This incremental approach takes advantage of the brain's plasticity and avoids the shock of demanding too much too soon. As students build the capacity to focus, he writes, unruly and silly behavior becomes less appealing because students begin looking forward to getting into their work. He frames this ability to focus not as innate work ethic but as a trainable skill that gives students a lasting advantage in whatever they pursue.
points: In an age of constant digital distraction, the ability to focus on one task for an extended period is framed as an increasingly valuable 'superpower.'
Lengthy independent practice is described as a core SCM principle that builds comprehension, skill acquisition, and self-confidence.
Focus stamina should be built gradually: start with a manageable amount of independent work time and add roughly a minute per week.
When diminishing returns appear, teachers should hold at that duration for two to three weeks before increasing further.
As focus stamina grows, students look forward to their work, which makes unruliness and silliness far less appealing.
quotes: In this age of distraction . . . Of smartphones and Instagram. Of texting and Snapchat. Of clickbait and information overload.
This is one reason why lengthy independent practice is a core principle of SCM.

The idea is to start conservatively with an amount your students can handle without trouble and increase gradually from there. In this way, you take advantage of the remarkable plasticity of the human brain.
It can even improve behavior, because your students will actually begin looking forward to getting down to work—making, in comparison, unruliness, silliness, and the like far less enticing.
It’s a skill cultivated by teachers who know that it isn’t bouncing from one thing to next, multitasking, or trying to mimic worldly distractions that are the secret to deep learning.
